sentences.text: Machimosaurus teeth are characterized by a rounded, blunt apex and stout morphology, making them easily distinguishable from other teleosaurid teeth.

Fossils of this animal have been found in the semi-aquatic deposits of Oker, Lower Saxony, Germany, dating to the Kimmeridgian age, and it is also found alongside Steneosaurus in Titonian age deposits in western France.
Machimosaurus is the largest known crocodyliform from the Jurassic period.
Machimosaurus rex, described in 2016 from Tunisia, is the largest known teleosaurid, estimated at 9.6 meters long and weighing nearly three tons.
Fossil turtles from the Kimmeridgian Solothurn Limestone in northern Switzerland show bite marks and contain chipped Machimosaurus teeth embedded in their shells.
Machimosaurus went extinct during the Hauterivian, making it the last of the teleosaurids.
The genus Machimosaurus was named by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1837 after he originally named isolated conical, blunt teeth from Switzerland as Madrimosaurus hugii.
In 1838, von Meyer corrected the misspelling to Machimosaurus, derived from Greek words meaning "pugnacious lizard".

Bite marks on a sauropod femur from Switzerland match teeth of Machimosaurus hugii, suggesting it fed on sauropods, and bite marks on a Cetiosauriscus femur from the early Kimmeridgian of Switzerland also match the known teeth of Machimosaurus hugii.

Morphofunctional analysis of the skull suggests Machimosaurus specialized in eating turtles, and fossil turtles from the Kimmeridgian Solothurn Limestone in northern Switzerland show bite marks and contain chipped Machimosaurus teeth embedded in their shells.
The teeth of Machimosaurus are morphologically adapted for seizing and crushing hard prey, and morphological comparisons of its teeth confirm Machimosaurus was adapted to capture and crush hard prey.

Vertebrae articulations indicate Machimosaurus lived in open seas, swimming via lateral tail undulations while using limbs for steering and balance, and based on vertebrae zygapophysis joints, Machimosaurus likely lived in open seas, swimming with lateral tail undulations while its legs steered and balanced the body.

Large basioccipital tubera suggest well-developed head and neck muscles, assisting Machimosaurus in diving, and Machimosaurus likely had well-developed muscle depressions on its head and neck for downward movements and a large basioccipital tuberosity attachment site, which were likely very useful for Machimosaurus to submerge itself.
The genus includes species such as M. hugii, M. mosae, M. nowackianus, M. buffetauti, and M. rex.
Machimosaurus belongs to the family Teleosauridae, is classified within the suborder Thalattosuchia, belongs to the subfamily Machimosaurini, and is classified within the family Machimosauridae.

Machimosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian and Tithonian) and Early Cretaceous periods, lived between the Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian and Tithonian) and Early Cretaceous (Berriasian and Hauterivian) periods, and lived between 165.3 and 113.2 million years ago during the Callovian to Aptian periods.
Fossils of Machimosaurus have been found in Switzerland, England, France, Germany, Portugal, and Tunisia.
It is uncertain whether ichnofossils of a gigantic crocodylomorph from Spain belong to Machimosaurus.
